findings.asked: Take logs, plot, find k and A, then predict.
findings.wentWrong: Nearly everyone took logs; scales were often poor so points bunched; k came from the gradient, but A was frequently given as log A; some put log values into the exponential equation.
findings.rule: The intercept is log A - undo the log to get A.

findings.asked: Log-log graph, find a and b, predict, state an assumption.
findings.wentWrong: Values not to 3 d.p.; log r on the wrong axis; a given as log a; predictions outside the data range not questioned; the radius given for the diameter; the assumption misunderstood.
findings.rule: A prediction must lie within the range of the data you plotted.

findings.wentWrong: Rounding, plotting and axis labels cost marks; some inverted the gradient for n; a left as log a.
findings.rule: n = gradient (rise over run in log units), a = 10 to the intercept.

findings.asked: Log-log graph with a contextual final part.
findings.wentWrong: Rounding, plotting and labelling again; some inverted the gradient or used the wrong equation for k; the final mark was lost by rounding down when the context required rounding up.
findings.rule: Round the final answer according to the context, not automatically down.

findings.asked: Log-log table, plot, gradient, find v and k, predict.
findings.wentWrong: Two decimal places instead of three, inaccurate plotting, missing axis labels; a few inverted the gradient or swapped k and v; some used a log equation for k unnecessarily.
findings.rule: Gradient gives the power; the intercept gives log of the constant.

ruleToRemember: Take logs to the stated decimal places, plot with labelled axes and a sensible scale, gradient = the power, intercept = log of the constant (undo it), and check predictions sit inside the data range.
